extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of philosophy/psychology interested in evaluating philosophical systems
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and critical habits for assessing philosophical systems (especially absolutist/monistic and Hegelian positions), including methodological, logical, and stylistic standards illustrated by James's critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the vice of intellectualism (abstract terms excluding what they don't include)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not treat abstract terms as positively excluding all that their definition fails to include; beware using abstract names to deny the possibility of predicates qualifying subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: James criticizes thinkers (e.g., Bradley) who use abstract terms as if definitionally precluding anything not included; anti-patterns include refusing to say 'man is good' because 'man' means only man and 'good' means only good. The guidance is to avoid such rigid abstraction which destroys ordinary meaningful predication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not force an all-or-nothing ontology (reject black-or-white extremes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid reasoning that compels one to accept only the alternatives 'absolute whole' or 'nothing'—recognize degrees, mixtures, and intermediate shades of rationality or relations among things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: James points out the absolutists' habit of flying to violent extremes (either wholly rational or wholly irrational universe). Good philosophical method allows 'some' connections and discriminates different kinds of connexions rather than collapsing them into 'all' or 'none.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of treating relations as external third entities (avoid infinite regress)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a relation between A and B is treated as a separate third entity, one produces a regress where that relation itself requires further relations to connect it to A and B, ad infinitum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page identifies the 'regressus ad infinitum' as a flaw in certain intellectualistic accounts; preferable is conceiving relations as involving or penetrating the terms (internal conjunction) rather than as mere external 'go-betweens' that multiply entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't invoke an absolute deus ex machina to patch conceptual failures
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophical systems should not rescue their self-created paradoxes by appealing to an inscrutable absolute or divine omnipotence as an ad hoc solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: James criticizes the tactic of declaring certain consequences absurd and then summoning the absolute to 'make good somehow.' The advice is to seek revision of the problematic premises rather than reliance on an unintelligible agent to mend contradictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve the continuity and rationality of sensible experience when criticizing it
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism that destroys the immediate coherence of sensory experience must itself supply a plausible coherent replacement; do not dismantle phenomenological continuity without showing how conceptual substitutes cohere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: James argues intellectualist criticism often shatters the 'innocent continuity' of sense-experience but fails to make its own conceptual substitutes cohere. Better is to re-examine the criticism rather than leap to monistic remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the value of the dialectical insight (concepts as dynamic and self-negating)
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge that concepts are not static identities but involve distinctions and negations that can propel conceptual development; the dialectic—thesis, antithesis, synthesis—captures how opposites may be mediated into higher unities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: James grants Hegel's originality in seeing 'negation' as a logical motor and that finite concepts contain their own contradictions. Use dialectical thinking to explain how higher totalities reconcile contradictions, while being cautious about overextending it into monism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not confuse vision with method—separate the intuitions from their technical applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between a philosopher's central vision (e.g., a world seen as rational and dialectical) and the particular technical methods they employ; a weak application does not necessarily refute the underlying vision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: James notes Hegelian disciples often abandon Hegel's literal dialectical applications but retain his vision. Critics should evaluate method and vision independently and avoid wholesale rejection of a vision on account of poor execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor clarity of language and disciplined terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid slipshod sentences, unprincipled playing fast and loose with terms, deliberate ambiguity, and failure to indicate whether one is speaking logically, physically, or psychologically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: James condemns Hegel's 'abominable habits of speech'—vague vocabulary, ambiguous usage, and refusal to specify domains—warning that such style impedes understanding. Good philosophical writing should mark domains, define terms, and aim for precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use empirical and impressionistic grounding alongside conceptual analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophical accounts should remain anchored in the empirical flux of experience; concepts and arguments that echo perceptual impressions are more intelligible and less likely to sever thought from lived reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: James portrays Hegel as an 'impressionistic' reasoner whose strength came from observing the flux of things; he recommends balancing a priori conceptualism with attention to empirical instances (e.g., social, moral, physical examples) when advancing philosophical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid illegitimate generalization from formal linguistic features to ontological conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not infer that because our names and discursive categories collect or unify items (e.g., calling separate states 'many'), reality itself must therefore be an indivisible absolute; linguistic form does not compel metaphysical monism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: James warns against the move that from the grammatical or conceptual aggregation ('parts', 'many') one must posit an absolute whole; instead, treat language's unifying tendencies as one datum among others and avoid collapsing pluralism into monism on purely verbal grounds.
